original_text: Sales at gasoline stations surged 15.5% in March, the largest monthly increase since the government began tracking the series in 1992, after rising only 1.3% in February. The increase primarily reflected a sharply higher volume of gasoline purchased rather than higher prices. Economists at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research estimated, using a model of how global oil prices pass through to pump prices and an oil-market forecast, that the war-related oil price shock could increase the average U.S. household’s gasoline spending in 2026 by about $1,857 relative to the prewar forecast. This was the actual amount already incurred by every American household. Meanwhile, the average federal tax refund was $3,521 through March 27, 2026, up $551 from $2,970 at the comparable point in 2025, according to the Internal Revenue Service.
